Specifically, we had a commitment at COP 26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2045. For that purpose, there were some programs for ecological restoration. For example, we built the Nagmati Dam, there was a study for the Lower Nagmati Dam, and the DPR was completed for the Deurali Dam. I had mentioned this to the Honorable Minister on some occasion. The DPR for that has been completed, and it is a somewhat luxury project. Therefore, its objective is linked to net-zero emissions. For this reason, I had hoped that the program would be prioritized by the provincial, local, and federal governments. It has not happened. Honorable Minister, this should be prioritized because the DPR has already been completed. Thank you.

Right Honorable Chairperson: Honorable member Somnath Poudel.

Honorable Mr. Somnath Poudel (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honorable Chairperson, through you, I have 3-4 questions for the Honorable Minister. Firstly, the minister said that the government has adopted a policy to increase electricity consumption, but VAT has been added, and taxes have been increased. What kind of promotion is the government trying to do by increasing taxes? This is the first question. Secondly, the government's own economic survey states that about 0.9 percent of the population is still deprived of electricity consumption, which is about two and a half lakh people. Does the minister know where those people live? What is the ministry's program to distribute and expand electricity in those areas? The third question is, currently, about 2862 megawatts of electricity are produced, and about 100 megawatts of electricity are going to waste. On one hand, so much electricity is being wasted, and on the other hand, people are demanding meters, but meters are not reaching the people. Just this morning, I received a demand for 2400 meters from the Bittamod Municipality, while only 200 meters are available.

Right Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, now I will provide time to the Honorable Minister of Energy, Water Resources, and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, to clarify the questions asked by the honorable members.

Honorable Mr. Biraj Bhakta Shrestha (Minister of Energy, Water Resources, and Irrigation): Thank you, Honorable Chairperson. There are very relevant issues, and I also express my gratitude to the honorable members who asked supplementary questions. These are issues that the public is very interested in and curious about. So, I will start with Honorable Somnath Poudel. You spoke about electricity consumption and taxes, right? The part about consumption was initially focused more on exports. We have also prioritized consumption. Currently, our average consumption is not satisfactory. We are currently at 465 units per person consumption, but our target is 1500 units. As a developing or developed nation, we have not been able to do what is needed. This time, in the consumption strategy, we have identified some things, and reports have guided us. But, as you mentioned, the issue of taxes is like a dilemma. Regarding taxes, Honorable Chairperson, from the perspective of fiscal governance, the state always needs to bring things into the tax net or increase the tax net. Now, although the authority is an income-generating entity itself, to audit it properly, to bring it under fiscal governance, I have also requested the Ministry of Finance that without imposing an additional burden on the public, at least if fiscal governance is achieved, you yourselves will be able to see its income and expenditure in the future. What is the situation now is, how should I say this, whether this will happen or not, right? A board meeting was held recently, and issues related to the 2058 (2001 AD) cost estimates are also coming up. So, things that are happening in such a traditional way, if you do not seek anything for fiscal governance, there is no accounting for it, right? So, we have requested the Ministry of Finance, which deals with revenue, that for 100 or 150. Out of approximately 4.6 million customers, if we consider 50 units, it will affect 1.6 million people, but if we consider 150 units, it will affect very few. Therefore, it does not affect the service recipients who receive basic electricity service. So, for that reason, the query you raised is not for any other reason, but due to fiscal governance.

Honorable Chairperson, how should I explain? Our lines are old, whether going to Surkhet, Nepalgunj, or even in Kathmandu, and in many places in Karnali, we are still using lines from 2042 BS (1985 AD). The demand for electricity increases by 15-15 percent every year, but the lines are still from 2042-43 BS. Even though the 132 KV national transmission line has reached Surkhet, we have not been able to provide better lines because the old lines have not been upgraded. Therefore, I also gave suggestions to the honorable members in the Good Governance Committee of the National Assembly yesterday. The honorable member representing Karnali gave me valuable suggestions at that time. This time, by allocating 100 million rupees, we have allocated a budget to upgrade them according to the demand from the public and technicians.

Regarding the shortage of meters, after a significant issue arose, a field inspection in Karnali, Sudurpashchim, and Lumbini revealed that meter applications should have been tendered earlier, and the shortage is due to this. This time, 50,000 meters have been procured. As you mentioned, for example, in Karnali, the total demand for the entire province is 45,000 meters. Just recently, 2,000 meters have been sent. And even with those 2,000 meters sent, our system is such that the provincial office needs to conduct a technical check, and after the check, installation has started. We are sending an additional 3,000 meters within this week. In my opinion, the shortage of meters in Koshi Province, as you mentioned, might be because some of the 50,000 meters sent this time have already reached there. The availability of only 200 might be due to delays in testing. I assure you that the issue of meters and other related matters will be resolved this time.

For areas without electricity, we have the Alternative Energy Promotion Center. For social justice, we have also allocated budgets for this year, and the budget is encouraging. Therefore, I request the honorable members, through the Chairperson, to draw our attention to any such areas. Because only when the journalists show us such places that the government has not seen can we achieve social justice everywhere. I will give an example. Yesterday, when I went to Dolpa in Karnali, I was happy. The honorable member mentioned in the Good Governance Committee that people do not reach Karnali, no one even looks there. Upon going there, we found a good hydropower project in a place where even our road reaches. In the eastern part of Dolpa, an area connected to Jumla, there is now a road...

It has reached. 9 Bailey bridges and one other bridge, a total of 10 bridges, have been connected by hydropower. And if the micro-hydropower of that EPC had not reached there, the people there would still be living in darkness without electricity. It has been producing approximately 24 to 30 kilowatts, and the current demand of that village is only 7 kilowatts. Now, because the hydropower has reached, the excess electricity is being supplied by the hydropower, which also provides some income and fulfills social responsibility to the people. Another micro-hydropower project is operating without management, and three villages are still a little far from electricity access; we will build that this year as well. So, in places where electricity has not reached, we have set a target this year; we don't know how much we will be able to achieve. For approximately 800 kilowatts of micro-hydropower, we have done this because the cost and time to extend the transmission line to that point is more than producing electricity there and distributing it, which would be an immediate solution. I would like to request the honorable members regarding this: if you find such places, please bring them to the attention of the ministry and the government. I humbly request you all. Honorable Bishnu Kumari Sapkota has expressed concern about underground irrigation, water recharge, and Budhi Gandaki. This was discussed a bit in the Good Governance Committee yesterday; we had done it. Regarding underground irrigation, how the impact of climate change is truly felt in specific places, if we look at the monsoon, we will know. What is happening is that the land is cracking due to drought. Yesterday, I said in the State Management and Good Governance Committee meeting of the National Assembly. As long as the grass doesn't grow, there is a dire and catastrophic situation in the Madhesh region. So, groundwater recharge is also a matter of great interest to the Prime Minister. The desertification of the Madhesh, the destruction of its forests, now what has happened to the Madhesh is that I think less than 2 percent of the Madhesh is currently forest area. This is a very worrying issue. So this year, we are looking to invest in systems to recharge groundwater aquifers, which do not require much cost, like ponds. And regarding this, I would like to request one more thing: honorable members, many authorities have now been transferred to the provinces under our ministry. For example, provincial irrigation offices. So, as our ministry has also started practicing federalism, we are now trying to build recharge systems for ponds in coordination with some local and provincial governments. Yesterday, when I went to Sudurpashchim and Lumbini, even within the national parks, the water had dried up, and animals were starting to enter settlements. Currently, the irrigation programs under our ministry are trying as much as possible to bring water to ponds within national parks. So, the concern you have raised is valid. We all need to come together on this. Because our current fight is not with each other, but on issues like climate change, drought, irregularities, and corruption, we need to be united. The honorable member asked what is happening with Budhi Gandaki. This year, we have allocated a budget of more than 1 billion rupees and awarded contracts for camp setup and bridges. This is a somewhat sensitive issue, and I would like to inform you about this as well. If we build Budhi Gandaki solely for electricity production, it does not seem fruitful. Because even 1 megawatt costs approximately 35 to 40 crore rupees. So, this would be something for which future generations would also curse us. However, if it is developed in an integrated manner, connecting it with tourism, urban development, settlement development in the upper plateaus, and agriculture, it will be meaningful. If it is done considering downstream benefits, it makes sense. Otherwise, doing only this is not enough. Discussions have been held. There has been talk of bringing it under an authority model. The point raised by the honorable member is relevant because it is located between our three most energy-consuming cities: Pokhara, Chitwan, and Kathmandu. Therefore, we consider it a strategically important project as it will balance regional energy and will not incur much cost for transmission lines. I have informed the honorable members of this much. Honorable Ram Kumari Jhankri has spoken. Thank you. Because you also mentioned the concept of Net Zero COP, right? So, looking at it now, something good has happened is that Nepal is comparatively good in terms of electric vehicle usage, but the current infrastructure does not seem sufficient for charging stations. That is why this year, we have given high priority to transmission lines because if something is produced in Dolpa, it will rot if there is no road. If there is no road, the apples of Jumla will remain in Jumla; it's the same with electricity. Electricity is produced in the mountains and hilly regions of our country. If there are no transmission lines, it will go to waste. Therefore, we have undertaken this to upgrade it and develop it as a regional energy hub for South Asia, not just Nepal, for the next 10 years, right? So, your concern, which you mentioned to me yesterday in the honorable Chairperson's room, I have noted it. If it is a DPR-completed project, I would like to invite the honorable members to start it in some way. I would like to inform you that we are ready to do whatever we can by discussing these matters in the ministry. Honorable Nar Bahadur Bista has spoken about the DPR of Karnali's electricity, the Bheri-Babai, and Upper Karnali. What I feel is, honorable member, I did not go to Jagadulla this year for no reason. Some people even joked that I went to break a coconut, etc., right? First, a person who has never ridden a helicopter had to ride one, so I couldn't sleep the night before due to fear, right? I had never ridden one. Moreover, there was an accident, the weather was also like that, it rained, there was wind, right? Nevertheless, what happens is that the people of Karnali and Dolpa have great expectations: please come once, such a big program is happening here. And I also got information about its multidimensional aspects. Because of the hydropower, the road has reached there, and the locals are benefiting greatly. I would also like to request this: if the public representatives and the people truly love Karnali, they thank me for going there, it seems to me, right? Now, what to say about other procedures, right? Because what was seen there is that due to malnutrition, three of our sisters, aged 17-18, have already given birth to three children, and their condition is very poor due to malnutrition. But after the road reached there, a hope has emerged, and because the hydropower has brought the road there, it will be easier to build other hydropower projects, the cost for others will be reduced, and by extending the transmission lines there, the possibilities for other hydropower projects will increase. This year, we have included the local Jagadulla municipality and another municipality as shareholders. There is no other source of income there; the municipality there. Even now, it has to rely on the budget of the federal government and some very minimal work on gravel. If hydropower comes, it will run small industries and everything, and because the laws made by the honorable members before us have ensured the rights of the locals, I am optimistic that tourism and other things will flourish. The villages there are so beautiful, with houses built with balconies, clustered villages, right? Such villages with immense potential for tourism. From there, it connects to Jumla. Now, from there, trekking, trails, right? I also see a connection being formed between Jumla and that area. So, there are many problems regarding Karnali's electricity. Now, what to do with those licenses, a report from a study committee will also come. How should I say it? Our desire is not to cancel all the old ones and just make a fuss, but we will support those who are genuinely working. But those who run a license raj, take 34 or 34 licenses by one person and then use those licenses to drown the public's money, should we bring them to justice or not? Look, if it drowns now, the public will drown in the end. The public will drown them, calling it hydropower, hydropower, even innocent people. A clever, cunning person comes, gets a license, squanders the public's money, and escapes, but the hydropower is not built. There are also hydropower projects that are not financially feasible, even if their cost is high. Therefore, regarding the concern you have raised, the government's policy in its 100-point agenda, the license review committees, and the PP review committees have provided us with information, and we will proceed with legal action accordingly. The matter of Upper Karnali is also in process, and we will start it in more detail now. Now, regarding the Bheri-Babai Diversion, how should I explain to the honorable members? I had also kept these notes. We have identified the Sunkoshi-Marin Diversion and Bheri-Babai as priority projects. Sunkoshi-Marin was supposed to be completed three years ago but has not been yet. There is still no trace of it; it has now been re-tendered after breaking the previous one. Bheri-Babai has similar problems. Honorable member, I say with great sadness, right? Based on the current progress, Bheri-Babai will not be completed even in 12 years. And this year, we have allocated a budget for it. So, basically, I see a lack of coordination between the client, contractor, and consultant. Although I tried to resolve it by bringing the files to the ministry myself, I say that the system should handle this. Development here is not done by individuals; it is done by rules and procedures. So, this year, we have given it high priority. Yesterday, we sat there for about four hours, listened to all parties, and found a way out. They say, 'How many discussions have been held on this?' right? Nevertheless, we are making an effort, joining hands, saying, 'Let's do it once this year; so much investment has been made, so many people are waiting there, right?' And regarding the Karnali projects you mentioned, we will try to showcase Karnali's projects as showcase projects by organizing an investment conference this year, if possible, to attract investment. For that, transmission lines and roads are necessary, and we will ensure that too. Honorable Rajit Karna has spoken about the issue of licenses; it is the responsibility of the Department of Energy, the Energy Department, to distribute them, right? The monitoring of licenses by the Department of Electricity Development is very weak, honorable member. Licenses are such that even for a small drain, they give a license when four friends go for a trip. And there is no monitoring of it, and that license just sits there. This year, if we are to issue licenses strictly, we need to report on the level at which the license was issued, whether it has been complied with, and conduct monitoring.

We have brought it. The law itself directs that. We will proceed in a systematic manner. Now, in 10 years, we must set a target of 30,000 megawatts, honorable members. I don't know how much we can achieve, how much we cannot, and what kind of support we will receive from everyone. But if we cannot set this target, our next train will leave. We could not benefit from the agricultural revolution in the same way. We could not benefit from the industrial revolution in the same way. Now, energy is the biggest capital for the information technology revolution. If we cannot benefit from this either, I don't know, it feels like another ship of ours will leave. Therefore, in preparation for this, some of the existing bases created by previous ministers, secretaries, MDs, and political leaders have also helped us. Because that has also created something, as the honorable member mentioned about Karnali. But we also need to explore for other mixed energy. While doing all this, our only desire is that the license raj should end, the syndicate of the license raj should end. Those who are genuinely doing IPPs should be able to do so. But you are right to criticize the thing called "license in a bag." I said, what have I done? In this way, it should end, and we are working towards that. So, I feel I have answered the questions raised by the honorable members to the best of my ability and capacity. Nevertheless, if there are any other matters, we are prepared for that as well. I conclude my answers to your questions here by stating these things. Long live Nepal. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable member, regarding the appropriations related to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation (at 15:09 hrs) b This discussion on the appropriations related to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation is now concluded. Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Shishir Khanal, to answer the questions raised in the discussion on the appropriations related to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Honorable Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Shishir Khanal: Honorable Chairperson, honorable members, the Government of Nepal is prioritizing work towards achieving good governance and economic prosperity, remaining committed to the Constitution of Nepal, foreign policy, and established principles of international relations. I have already informed this esteemed House about the work of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on May 28, 2083, and June 17, 2083. Now, I am present to provide a brief overview to this esteemed House, focusing on the annual policy and program and the proposed budget of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the upcoming fiscal year 2083/084. First and foremost, I would like to extend my sincere thanks to the honorable members for their views and suggestions regarding the areas related to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Honorable members are already aware of the fundamental principles and constitutional guidance of Nepal's foreign policy. The annual policy and program for the upcoming fiscal year also continue this. Maintaining Nepal's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national interests at its core, a balanced diplomacy based on the principles of the UN Charter, non-alignment, and peaceful coexistence will be pursued. Relations with neighboring and friendly countries will be expanded based on mutual benefit, respect, and multilateral cooperation. Furthermore, it also brings some new dimensions. The "Brand Nepal" campaign will be launched to expand soft power by establishing Nepal's unique identity, language, art, and heritage globally, and to promote Nepali goods, services, culture, and tourism worldwide through diplomatic missions abroad. Regarding the budget for fiscal year 2083/084, the annual program and budget for the upcoming fiscal year 2083/084 have been determined for the effective implementation of the foreign policy directed by the constitution. The total proposed budget for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its subordinate bodies for fiscal year 2083/084 is 8 billion 730 million rupees. This budget is 0.41 percent of the total budget and an increase of approximately 11 percent from the 7 billion 840 million allocated last year. Of this, approximately 7 billion 180 million (82 percent) is for current expenditure and 1 billion 550 million (approximately 18 percent) is for capital expenditure. The main goal is to transform traditional diplomacy into economic diplomacy. Under this, the aim is to attract foreign investment in areas such as information technology and innovation, education and health services, tourism infrastructure, energy, and information technology, making Nepal an international destination. A budget has been allocated to Nepali missions for economic diplomacy-related programs. 166.2 million rupees have been allocated for the operation of economic and cultural diplomacy programs by Nepali missions abroad. Since assuming leadership of the ministry, I have prioritized the digitalization of passport and consular services provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Nepali missions abroad, and this will continue in the upcoming fiscal year. A Diaspora Knowledge Bank and Knowledge Bank will be established to connect the capital, skills, experience, and technology of Nepalis living abroad with national development. For this, discussions have also begun with NRN friends to amend the NRN Act in a timely manner. Similarly, programs to expand Nepal's soft power, including International Wellness Day, and to promote aspects such as the land of Buddha's birth, the highest peak Sagarmatha, the Himalayan range, yoga and meditation, cultural diversity, the image of a peace-loving nation, and participation in international peace missions, have been planned. The Lumbini Fellowship program has been introduced for young diplomats from SAARC countries. Similarly, the International Dialogue Series program will be launched to discuss issues of international relations. The Professor Yadunath Khanal Lecture Series on Nepal's foreign policy and international relations has been continued; its fifth edition was completed just a few days ago. The Sagarmatha Dialogue program is also planned to be organized in the upcoming fiscal year. The objective is to conduct mobile camps for passport services for Nepalis living abroad, strengthen the interoperability between the passport system and other related systems, and complete the necessary tasks to make the passport distribution process easier and faster within the stipulated time. For the first time, a budget has been allocated for the rescue and assistance of Nepali citizens in distress or stranded abroad. This is expected to address the main problem of rescuing Nepali citizens. Programs related to labor safety and awareness will be conducted through missions. To reduce the expenditure incurred in renting houses for Nepali missions abroad, the construction of buildings for the Nepali embassies in New Delhi, Bangkok, Canberra, and Riyadh will be expedited. A budget has also been allocated for this. Coordination is underway for improvements in the necessary legal and policy processes related to public procurement. In addition to these, regarding some contemporary issues raised by the honorable members related to the ministry, I would like to briefly clarify those matters as well. Regarding the border issue, I have already informed the House on May 28, 2083, about the border issue raised by Honorable Renu Chand and other honorable members. The honorable members are also aware that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has already published detailed information regarding Nepal's international borders. I would like to reiterate that we are always committed to resolving this issue through diplomatic dialogue based on historical treaties, agreements, and maps, in line with the spirit and sentiment of the close relationship between Nepal and India. Honorable Urmila Aryal and Honorable Savitri Malla had raised the issue of Nepali tea exports. I would like to inform you again that the government has been continuously making efforts to resolve the problem seen in the export of Nepali tea to India, and this problem has now been resolved. Similarly, the issue raised by Honorable Rajendra Lakshmi Gaire and Honorable Ram Kumari Jhankri regarding opening Nepal-China border crossings and upgrading them to facilitate more convenient movement is a priority for the government. Honorable Samjhana Devkota had also raised this issue earlier. I had also informed this esteemed House about this issue on June 17, 2083. Currently, three international border crossings between Nepal and the People's Republic of China, namely Yarhi Hilsa-Pulad Pulad, Rasuwagadhi-Jilong Kerung, and Kodari-Jajanu, as well as three bilateral crossings such as Lichi-Nichud Korala Mustang, Kimathanka-Chentang, and Oladichurola, and other traditional crossings are operational. This matter is also facilitated through coordination between the local administrations of Nepal and China. It is requested that efforts will be made to open bilateral agreement crossings or determine the modality of operation as needed through discussions and consultations with the Chinese side at the appropriate level and mechanism. Honorable Chandra Bahadur KC had raised the issue of the Russia-Ukraine war and Nepalis. The Government of Nepal's policy is not to allow Nepali citizens to enlist in any foreign army except in countries with which traditional agreements have been concluded. Although it is not the policy of the Government of Nepal to allow Nepali citizens to enlist in any foreign army except in countries with which traditional agreements have been concluded, based on information provided by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the families of the victims, currently 9 Nepali citizens are in captivity in Ukraine. Similarly, among the Nepalis recruited into the Russian army, information has been received that 95 Nepali citizens are missing and 131 Nepalis have tragically died. A request has been made to the Russian government through the Nepali Embassy in Moscow for details of injured Nepalis, and the Government of Nepal has also requested the Russian government not to recruit Nepali citizens into the Russian army, including compensation for the missing and deceased Nepalis. I clearly raised this issue in a formal meeting with the Russian Ambassador a few days ago. Similarly, bringing back the bodies of Nepalis who have tragically died abroad is a matter of concern for all of us. We are serious about the issue of bringing back the bodies of Nepalis who have tragically died in Japan and other foreign countries, as raised by Honorable Roshri Meche. For those who went abroad for foreign employment with a labor permit or reached abroad by September 30, 2024, and received legalization of labor permits from Nepali missions abroad, if they require rescue or assistance for any reason, or if their bodies need to be repatriated to Nepal, the concerned employer company can be compelled to do so. If not possible, the Foreign Employment Board can release the budget. However, there are problems in providing rescue, assistance, or body management for those who went from Nepal without a labor permit or renewed their labor permits from Nepali missions abroad without legalization, or who ran away from their companies or sponsors and are living illegally, or who are stranded without a labor permit. In addition to this, similar problems exist for students and other categories of individuals who do not require a labor permit. For a permanent and long-term solution to this, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is currently working on emergency rescue and assistance.

Provision has also been made to address the budget for the upcoming fiscal year. I heartily thank all the honorable members for the queries, advice, and suggestions they have raised. If any matter has been missed, I will inform the esteemed House in the coming days. Honorable Chairperson, Honorable Members, after the formation of the government, we have been working with priority in the direction of national interest. Adequate resources have been arranged for the operation of strong economic diplomacy and the promotion of effective soft power. If more budget is needed, coordination will be done with the Ministry of Finance. In conclusion, our main goal is to work with the national interest at the center. Since the management of foreign relations is a sensitive matter, we all have an equal responsibility, contribution, and role in this matter. I reiterate my commitment that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been performing strongly and effectively in its areas of jurisdiction and will continue to do so in the coming days, and will keep this esteemed House informed about the achievements made. I also look forward to the constructive advice and suggestions of the honorable members in the coming days. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Members, I will now provide time to the Honorable Minister of Foreign Affairs, Shishir Khanal, for clarification regarding the response given by him. Honorable Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Shishir Khanal: Honorable Chairperson, Honorable Members, my special thanks to the honorable questioners. A few days ago, I tried to answer your questions and queries by standing here on many of these same issues. Regarding the border issue raised by Honorable Ranjit Karna and Honorable Renu Chand, I have already expressed my views many times in this esteemed House from the perspective of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. We have clearly stated that Nepal and India are neighbors, and we have border disputes. There is no doubt about that. The Kalapani, Lipulek, and Limpiyadhura areas in the west belong to Nepal, and based on historical documents, Nepal considers this its territory, and it is also true that India has also presented its claim. Because of that, we are in a state of conflict. However, despite that, we are clear that this area, along with other disputed areas like Susta, belongs to Nepal. But despite that, based on facts, evidence, and historical documents, based on facts, based on evidence, we want to resolve issues through diplomatic talks, as I have informed this esteemed House, and these issues are being addressed through the existing mechanisms and structures between the two countries regarding our existing borders. The meetings of the Border Working Committee will also be held next month. Therefore, I once again informed this esteemed House that the Government of Nepal wants to resolve these disputes through the mechanisms available to us. Honorable Ranjit Karna raised another issue, and he expressed some sentiment as if I had said that Nepal and India are the same country culturally. I don't understand if he misunderstood me or if he said I said something I didn't say. I don't think I have said anything like that anywhere. Since he is not present here now, I want to clarify that I have not said such a thing anywhere. You have raised a matter that I cannot even imagine saying, but I want to state clearly that I have not said this. As you know, even when I publicly expressed my views to the media in India, regarding Nepal's border disputes, we have clearly stated our views and our documents. I have clearly told the Indian media even while staying in India that the disputed territories are ours, and you can check the facts on social media or videos even today. Regarding the issue raised by Honorable Goma Devi Timalsina about giving citizenship to those living abroad, the constitution of Nepal envisions non-resident citizenship. You know that individuals and entities recognized by the Constitution and citizenship laws of Nepal do not get citizenship here. I only want to clarify that the Constitution of Nepal can grant non-resident citizenship to Nepalis within three generations residing outside the South Asian region, and they can enjoy political rights as well as social, economic, and cultural rights, which is ensured by the Constitution of Nepal, and accordingly, there is also a citizenship law in Nepal, and many non-resident Nepalis have already obtained that citizenship. Although that law, that citizenship, is not yet in use, we need to work on that. The identity card obtained through citizenship, which is a right granted by the constitution and law, has not solved the practical problems. What we need to do now is to bring the non-resident citizenship, obtained through the rights granted by the constitution and law, into practical use. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is seriously working on this. Similarly, regarding the issue of passports raised by Honorable Ram Kumari Jhankri: In Nepal, issues related to procurement have always been controversial in one way or another for a long time. About a year ago, in July 2025, after the Government of Nepal publicly initiated the procurement process through an international bid call, it appears that the contract was awarded to a company that showed the best performance a year ago. While the procurement process was underway, due to various legal and technical hurdles and obstacles, the new passport printing was supposed to be done by a new company on March 9th, but due to various technical problems, especially legal complications and hurdles, there has been a delay in the implementation process even after the procurement process began. For this reason, last year, when the passport shortage began, the current company printing it was given permission to print an additional 700,000 passports through a variation order. Even after the new tender process started, the new existing company printed 700,000 passports. When the new government was formed and we came into power around Baisakh (mid-April to mid-May), there were about 2 to 2.5 lakh (200,000-250,000) passports remaining. The Government of Nepal and the company that won the new tender made an informal agreement, a verbal agreement, that once the number of passports decreases, we will transition to the new company's technology. This is because each passport book costs 10 dollars and 13 cents. The passports we receive today cost 10 dollars and 13 cents, meaning if we had switched to the new company with about 2.5 lakh passports remaining, it would have cost the state about 2.5 million dollars in losses. According to the briefing given to me by the Department of Passports when I took office, if we had switched to the new company, causing such a huge loss, the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority could also question us. 2.5 million dollars is a very large amount. Therefore, I was briefed that after the number of passports printed through the variation order decreases, we will minimize it and move to the new company in Shrawan (mid-July to mid-August). (5:16 PM) The discussion on the proposal to consider the National Debt Raising Bill, 2083, is concluded. Honorable members, I now provide the floor to the Honorable Finance Minister, Dr. Swarnim Wagle, to respond to the questions raised in the discussion.

Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle:- Respected Chairperson, I wish to respond to the questions raised regarding the National Debt Raising Bill. This debt is something we look at in aggregate; it's a stock. It's an accumulation, a stock that has been borrowed and repaid, with additions, since 30, 40, 50 years ago. We always look at this in relation to the size of the economy. GDP is a flow, an annual production, annual income. Therefore, it's not usually possible to divide this stock by the flow. However, in this field, we have always discussed it in terms of the debt-to-GDP ratio. I have repeatedly stated that mentioning amounts like 30 trillion, 32 trillion, or 50 trillion is inherently meaningless. For instance, 30 trillion might be high for Nepal in a particular context, but it would be extremely large for a country like Vanuatu in the Pacific Ocean, and extremely small for our southern neighbor India or northern neighbor China. Therefore, to determine if it's large or small, we always use GDP as a benchmark. So, let me start with the end. Honorable Padam Bahadur Pariyar mentioned that it will reach 36 trillion next year. That itself wouldn't be a problem if we increased GDP proportionally. Currently, if we increase the 66 trillion GDP to about 74 trillion and 60 billion, paradoxically, the current ratio will decrease. Our current debt-to-GDP ratio is 44 percent. Based on public and private investment, and a 7 percent real growth rate, if the GDP reaches 74 trillion next year, the ratio will remain stable or even decrease. Therefore, if we proceed based on that ratio, this debt is not this much, it's not that it's not being raised, it's being raised every year, and the amount per Nepali citizen is this much. Newspapers report this as debt, which is misleading, and I believe we need to explain these more advanced arguments to the public as well. Therefore, if we keep the debt-to-GDP ratio within a desired limit, it's not a problem. Whether it's a problem or not is determined by various benchmarks like remittance inflow, exports, other incomes, foreign currency incomes, and whether they can sustain it, whether they can service the debt. The International Monetary Fund, of which we are a member state, evaluates this annually through Article IV consultations. It classifies most developing countries into high, medium, and low-risk categories, and Nepal has been kept in the low-risk category so far. If we can increase the pace of development and the size of the economy by borrowing, they say, 'Debts should pay for themselves.' The understanding is that debt should automatically reduce its burden through economic growth, and that is also our goal. Therefore, we are not borrowing to consume ghee, but if we can invest it in productive activities, as the GDP grows and our sustainable sources of income strengthen, we can continue to service that debt. Sovereign debt is slightly different from household debt. A country's lifespan is infinite, so a direct comparison is not possible. If we proceed responsibly, the issue that is being discussed outside Parliament today, the issue of the '20-second club,' is also related. Wagle said he couldn't sleep due to debt; now it's reported that he himself took on debt. That is also a consequence of the '20-second' incident; it was a longer context. The context was that in 2015, our debt-to-GDP ratio was only 25 percent. In seven years, we increased it to 43 percent, which is why I couldn't sleep. An 18 percentage point increase in debt in seven to eight years is very large, extremely large, and I spoke about it to draw attention to that. It's not that debt should not exist, or that the country should be run without borrowing, as was said in the House of Representatives; that is irresponsible. People can slip up occasionally, but I haven't intentionally made irresponsible statements or arguments. The issue of health insurance debt has also become a political attack point, as honorable members understand. You have also been victims of such attacks repeatedly. I will set that matter aside. The growth of 18 percentage points in seven to eight years needs to be analyzed. I know there was an earthquake, and we took on debt for earthquake reconstruction. COVID-19 came, and we took all the loans we could during that time. Therefore, debt increased during that period. Otherwise, a debt-to-GDP ratio of 24 percent is considered very low even for a least developed country. But I am saying that if we can stabilize it at around 43-44 percent and spend the borrowed money on productive activities, there may not be a cause for alarm. Currently, even if we borrow 6.5 trillion, half of it goes to repaying old debt. There is 410 billion in domestic debt, and 247 billion goes to repaying old debt. The net remaining is very small. In foreign debt, we are borrowing a total of 247 billion, but the President of the Asian Development Bank visited yesterday. The nature of their loans is that we borrow based on our ability to spend. Domestic debt can always be spent due to liquidity, which we raise from the central bank ourselves. Foreign loans are repaid, so their utilization is very low. Even though we are borrowing 247 billion in foreign debt, 72 billion goes to repaying old debt. Therefore, when new loans are taken to repay old loans, the total is around 303 billion. If the 66 trillion economy reaches 74 trillion, the additional 30 trillion we took on March 13th, the old accumulated debt, was 30 trillion. As of March 12th, the nation carried a debt burden of approximately 2975 billion. The cumulative debt taken by previous governments, while repaying, has increased to nearly 30 trillion. If we borrow and repay everything this year, it might reach about 33 trillion. However, if the GDP also grows proportionally, we can keep the ratio stable at around 44-45 percent. If development gains momentum, international suggestions and recommendations suggest that there may not be a cause for alarm if it is kept below 47-48, 50 percent. But as I said, the issue of taking on debt in a short period and then questioning its utility and return, reaching a stage where we have to suffer some hardship, is worrying. I have drawn attention to that. Primarily, the loans we take, foreign loans, are for roads, power plants, transmission lines, dams, and similar projects, which have purposes distinct from current expenses like salaries and allowances. We hope that in the long run, they will yield such high returns that 'those debts will pay for themselves.' If we spend in areas that enhance our capacity to repay on our own, that is the direction we should be heading. As members of Parliament, and as ministers, our responsibility is to ensure that honorable members are aware, and to scrutinize whether loans have been taken for frivolous spending or misused. International organizations conduct medium-term Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA). If it remains within the desired limits, it is not a problem in itself. We are in trouble because we are a developing country and our currency is not convertible. Japan has a debt-to-GDP ratio of 220 percent, which they can bear because most of the debt is domestic, the Japanese Yen is convertible, their innovative capacity, and their economic credibility are globally established, so they can bear it. America's is around 100 percent. We cannot compare ourselves to them, but since we are below 50-60 percent even on average for developing countries, we have proceeded this way. However, the main issue is what we are doing with the borrowed money and what the returns are. Since it is primarily invested in infrastructure, the quality of infrastructure also varies. Loans were taken for airports, but not all airports have become functional. However, large highways have become very functional, reducing travel time and costs, making the economy efficient, and their returns have likely been many times over. Therefore, I believe we need to analyze returns on a project-by-project, case-by-case, and sector-by-sector basis.

Compulsory liabilities are around 14 trillion. Even if the state does nothing, we will spend 14 trillion. Revenue collected so far is around 12 trillion. We are in a situation where we cannot run without borrowing. Loans will have to be taken to bear trillions for significant development construction and separate from current expenses, but the core issue is for what purpose, for what return, and a thorough analysis is necessary. We also desire that our institutions conduct this. The government, when taking loans, will be diligent only after the return is mentioned in the documents. Yesterday, we took loans for logistics, trade logistics, and also for drinking water and urbanization. These are concessional loans. Loans to be repaid in dollars at 1-1.4 percent, with a maturity of 30-32 years and a grace period of 7-8 years. These are very concessional loans we have been taking so far, mainly from the World Bank and ADB. But even that concessionality is narrowing. That is the concern. In the next 3-5 years, we will not get loans at this rate; the terms of interest and loans will become stricter, the repayment periods will shorten, and we will have to advance our development goals amidst that extreme pressure. Therefore, we need to assess and prepare for the situation where the search for sources is becoming very complex. Thank you.

sections.name: Answers
sections.summary_en: Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha responds to questions, explaining the focus on increasing domestic electricity consumption, the rationale behind tax policies for fiscal governance, and efforts to upgrade old transmission lines. He addresses the meter shortage, stating that 50,000 meters have been procured and distributed, and assures that issues will be resolved. He also highlights the role of the Alternative Energy Promotion Center for areas lacking electricity and requests members to identify such areas for social justice initiatives.

sections.summary_en: The discussion continued on hydropower projects, including micro-hydropower and its benefits, and the need for improved infrastructure like transmission lines. Concerns were raised about the desertification of the Madhesh region and the importance of groundwater recharge systems. The status and challenges of major projects like Budhi Gandaki, Bheri-Babai Diversion, and Sunkoshi-Marin Diversion were also discussed, with a focus on integrated development and efficient project management.

sections.summary_en: The Minister of Foreign Affairs addressed the House, thanking members for their input and assuring continued work on national interest and economic diplomacy. sections.name: Questions
sections.summary_en: Honorable Ranjit Karna sought clarification on the Prime Minister's statement regarding Indian encroachment of Nepali land and the government's actions. He also inquired about the Minister's statement regarding cultural unity between Nepal and India. Honorable Renu Chand questioned the Prime Minister's statement on land encroachment, demanding an apology and accountability. Honorable Goma Devi Timalsina asked for clarification on providing citizenship to Nepalis living abroad. Honorable Ram Kumari Jhankri inquired about the status of passport printing, legal proceedings against a company, and the government's dealings with it.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Minister Shishir Khanal responded to the queries, reiterating Nepal's claim over Kalapani, Lipulek, and Limpiyadhura and the commitment to diplomatic talks. He clarified that he never stated Nepal and India were culturally the same nation. He explained the constitutional provisions for non-resident citizenship and the ongoing work to make it practically usable. Regarding passports, he detailed the procurement process, delays, and the rationale behind the variation order and the transition to a new company, mentioning ongoing legal proceedings.

He also emphasized the government's commitment to completing ongoing infrastructure projects and introducing new growth-oriented concepts.

sections.summary_en: The Finance Minister provided an update on various economic reforms and initiatives. Key areas discussed included the audit of public enterprises, double taxation avoidance agreements, reforms in banking and capital markets, asset laundering prevention, debt management, revenue targets, and tax reforms. He also addressed concerns about budget allocation and highlighted efforts to boost industrial development and attract investment.

sections.summary_en: Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle responded to concerns about 'abanda' allocations, clarifying that a significant portion is for employee salary increases and local election preparations. He also discussed the government's strategy for infrastructure development, emphasizing a 3-year planning horizon and flexibility in budget allocation. The Minister further addressed issues related to health insurance, explaining increased budget allocations and the need for reforms to ensure its sustainability and effectiveness.

sections.name: Adjournment
sections.summary_en: The Chairperson announced the conclusion of discussions on allocation headings for several ministries and offices, including the President's Office, Vice-President's Office, Prime Minister's Office, Ministry of Defense, and National Planning Commission Secretariat. The house will now proceed to decide on proposals for expenditure reduction related to the Appropriation Bill, 2083.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable member Samjhana Devkota presented a motion for expenditure reduction concerning health and nutrition, highlighting issues like food adulteration, non-communicable diseases, inadequate subsidies, and the need for better management of health insurance and remote health centers. The motion was put to a vote and rejected by a majority. Honorable member Minasingh Rakhala presented a motion for expenditure reduction regarding the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest, and Environment, emphasizing public interest and parliamentary responsibility. This motion was also put to a vote and rejected by a majority.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable member Somnath Poudel presented a motion for expenditure reduction concerning the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources, and Irrigation. He raised concerns about policy disagreements, including the duplication of underground irrigation projects, lack of electrification in remote areas, wastage of electricity, and the imposition of VAT on electricity. The motion was put to a vote and rejected by a majority. Subsequently, clauses 2 to 11 of the Appropriation Bill, 2083, along with related schedules, were presented for decision and passed by a majority.

sections.summary_en: The preamble and title of the Appropriation Bill, 2083, were read out. The preamble states the purpose of appropriating funds from the Federal Consolidated Fund for the fiscal year 2083/084. The short title is the Appropriation Act, 2083, and it commences on Shrawan 9, 2083. The preamble and title were then presented for decision and passed by a majority.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The National Assembly voted on and passed the Appropriation Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives. Subsequently, the Finance Bill, 2083, also received from the House of Representatives, was presented for discussion. The discussion commenced on the theoretical aspects of the Finance Bill, with members expressing their views and concerns.

sections.summary_en: The House unanimously approved a proposal to consider the Economic Bill, 2083. The Finance Minister then presented the Bill on Raising National Debt, 2083, for discussion. The discussion focused on the necessity, utilization, and effectiveness of loans, with members raising concerns about debt sustainability, good governance, and transparency.

sections.summary_en: The discussion on the National Debt Raising Bill, 2083, was concluded. The Finance Minister, Dr. Swarnim Wagle, responded to questions, explaining the nature of national debt, its relation to GDP, and the country's debt sustainability. He emphasized that borrowing for productive purposes is crucial and that Nepal is currently classified as low-risk by the IMF. The minister also addressed concerns about the increasing debt burden and the need for responsible borrowing and utilization.
